title: Splitwise Debt Simplification
description: Model debts as a directed graph, implement the min-cash-flow algorithm, understand the NP-hard optimal solution vs greedy approximation tradeoffs.

segments.text: Five friends go on a trip. Alice paid for dinner, Bob paid for the hotel, Charlie paid for the rental car. At the end, everyone owes different amounts to different people. With five people and ten transactions, there could be twenty individual debts. Debt simplification reduces these to the minimum number of payments — often just four instead of twenty.

Model debts as a directed weighted graph. Each person is a node. An edge from Alice to Bob with weight fifty means Alice owes Bob fifty dollars. Multiple edges between the same pair can be netted: Alice owes Bob fifty, Bob owes Alice thirty means Alice owes Bob twenty. This netting step alone reduces complexity significantly.

Compute each person's net balance: total amount they're owed minus total amount they owe. If Alice's net balance is positive fifty, she's owed fifty. If Bob's is negative thirty, he owes thirty. The sum of all net balances is always zero — money is conserved. Debt simplification is really about matching creditors with debtors efficiently.

The min-cash-flow algorithm: find the person who owes the most and the person who's owed the most. Create a payment between them for the minimum of the two amounts. Reduce both balances. Repeat until all balances are zero. This greedy approach produces at most N minus one transactions for N people — much better than the original edge count.

The greedy algorithm gives N minus one transactions. But sometimes fewer are possible. If Alice owes Bob ten, Bob owes Charlie ten, and Charlie owes Alice ten, the optimal solution is zero transactions — the debts cancel out in a cycle. How would you detect and eliminate such cycles?
segments.thought_prompt: How do you detect and eliminate debt cycles to minimize the number of transactions below N-1?

segments.text: Finding the absolute minimum number of transactions is NP-hard — it reduces to the subset sum problem. For N people, you'd need to find all subgroups whose debts cancel internally and settle them separately. With five friends, brute force works. With one hundred friends, you need the greedy approximation. Splitwise uses the greedy algorithm for groups under fifty people.

Implementation: store expenses with payer, amount, and split participants. On each new expense, update the debt graph. When a user requests settlement, run the min-cash-flow algorithm on the current graph. Display suggested payments. Track which payments are completed and update balances accordingly. Use database transactions to prevent concurrent modification.

Support multiple split types: equal split divides evenly, percentage split uses custom ratios, exact amounts for unequal contributions, and shares-based splitting where some people pay double. Each type produces different debt edges. Unequal splits are the most common source of bugs — ensure rounding distributes the remainder fairly across participants.

Rounding errors accumulate. A hundred-dollar bill split three ways: thirty-three point thirty-three each leaves one cent unaccounted. Splitwise assigns the remainder to the person who paid — they effectively paid one cent more. Always use integer cents for calculations and define a deterministic remainder distribution rule.

Design the data model and simplification algorithm for a group expense tracker with one hundred users, thousands of expenses, and real-time balance updates. What are your storage and computation tradeoffs?
segments.thought_prompt: Design debt simplification for 100 users with real-time balance updates. Recompute on every expense?

segments.text: Debt simplification models expenses as a directed graph, computes net balances, and uses the min-cash-flow greedy algorithm to minimize transactions. The optimal solution is NP-hard, but greedy gives excellent results for practical group sizes. Handle split types carefully, use integer arithmetic for money, and distribute rounding remainders deterministically.
